The RCS peak value in the head direction of the aircraft decreases non-linearly as the sweep angle increases.
When the sweep angle is 0 degrees, the RCS peak value is 36.08 dBm2.
When the sweep angle is 18 degrees, the RCS peak value is 16.25% of the 0 degree value.
When the sweep angle is 33 degrees, the RCS peak value is 10.25% of the 0 degree value.
When the sweep angle is 42 degrees, the RCS peak value is 23.82% of the 0 degree value.
When the sweep angle is 54 degrees, the RCS peak value is 10.30% of the 0 degree value.
When the sweep angle is 66 degrees, the RCS peak value is 7.97% of the 0 degree value.
The azimuth angle corresponding to one of the RCS peak values is equal to the sweep angle of the wing leading edge.
When the sweep angle is 33 degrees, the arithmetic average RCS value between ±30 degrees is 0.644% of the value when the sweep angle is 0 degrees.
When the sweep angle is 42 degrees, the arithmetic average RCS value between ±30 degrees is 0.409% of the value when the sweep angle is 0 degrees.
As the sweep angle increases, the aircraft's detection probability by a ground-based radar decreases.
The variable-sweep wing aircraft model has features including single-seat, twin-engine, twin vertical tails, double S-shaped bend inlets, and three bomb bays.
The numerical simulation method was validated through a microwave anechoic chamber experiment using a 1:36 scale cast-aluminum model.
The key radar parameters used in the detection probability model include 7 degree lobe width, 300 Hz PRF, 30 deg/s scanning velocity, 10 MW transmit power, and 36 dB antenna gain.
The paper concludes that the 33 degree sweep angle provides a good balance between RCS reduction and other aircraft design considerations.
